note: Streaming loudness normalization as publicly described or widely measured; platforms change these without notice. 'documented' = the platform states it in its own help/artist pages (as of the date); 'approximate' = community measurements or older statements. Re-check before relying on an exact number.
lossy_overshoot_note: approximate: decoded lossy files (Ogg/AAC/Opus/MP3) commonly peak ~0.5-2 dB above the source's true peak, more for loud, bright masters

spotify.name: Spotify
spotify.detail: Default 'Normal' -14 LUFS (Loud -11, Quiet -19, user-selectable); quiet tracks are only turned up until their true peak reaches about -1 dBTP; Spotify asks for -1 dBTP masters (-2 dBTP if louder than -14 LUFS). Album mode normalizes the album as a whole.

apple_music.name: Apple Music
apple_music.detail: Sound Check normalizes to about -16 LUFS; on by default in recent Apple Music apps (it was off by default in older iTunes). Boost of quiet tracks is limited by peak headroom (exact rule not published).

youtube.name: YouTube
youtube.detail: Measured at about -14 LUFS; loud uploads are turned down, quiet ones are not turned up. Not officially documented as a number.

tidal.name: TIDAL
tidal.detail: Normalizes to about -14 LUFS (album-based by default); earlier statements said -16.

amazon_music.name: Amazon Music
amazon_music.detail: Measured around -14 LUFS (reports range -13 to -14); whether quiet tracks are turned up is unclear.

soundcloud.name: SoundCloud
soundcloud.detail: No loudness normalization: the file plays as loud as it is, so louder masters sound louder next to others. Lossy encoding still adds overshoot.
